strategy.summary: Vesmo Elektromotory is a sound, group-owned Czech motor maker supplying two IE3 motors under one framework agreement. On the 4 kW motor it is our cheaper 30% second source (Nordmark holds 70% at a higher price). On the 15 kW motor it is effectively our sole source, and the qualified alternative quoted far higher. Its prices sit only slightly above our should-cost of its own plant, so there is little room for price-downs; the real game is holding prices flat. Its copper is bought forward at fixed prices until March 2027, which it stated in writing and on a call, so a copper-driven increase has no basis before then. Expect a push for an increase or a copper index clause from Q2 2027. We are a small account to it, and it is reviewing small accounts and focusing on volume customers. Our growing, shared forecast and the option to move 4 kW quota from Nordmark are our main currency. Delivery and quality have slipped clearly (OTD well below target and peers, ppm up sharply, mostly on the 15 kW motor). Use this for a ppm commitment and a delivery commitment, not for price pressure. Its KAM can settle up to about 2% alone; above that the fortnightly pricing committee must approve. History shows it settles well below its ask. Watch the contract's renewal-notice and price-notice deadline in early October.
strategy.decision_maker: Key account manager negotiates and can settle price changes up to about 2% alone. Larger changes go to the pricing committee, which meets every two weeks. The sales director sets the portfolio strategy (focus on volume customers). Evidence on named individuals is thin.

price_view.reasoning: Both prices sit only slightly above our should-cost of its own plant, within the estimate error, and are back at their earlier level after a dip. On the 4 kW motor it is clearly cheaper than Nordmark; on the 15 kW motor the alternative is far dearer. So price-downs would hurt a supplier we depend on. The real room lies in avoiding increases: its copper is hedged until March 2027, labour and steel add only small amounts, and it historically settles well below its ask. Target a flat price through the hedge period. After that, accept at most a moderate, evidence-based step or a carefully based copper clause.

findings.text: Vesmo prices sit only slightly above our should-cost of its own CZ plant: part:350010 EUR 225.61 vs 221.47 (+1.9%), part:350012 EUR 601.27 vs 591.20 (+1.7%). Both are within the 5% estimate error, so its margin is thin to nil. There is little room to push price down without hurting supplier health. Using the sup:70510 DE-plant estimate (244.39) would show Vesmo selling below cost, but that estimate is for a different plant and must not be used against us.

Copper is the dominant driver: +47.7% in 12 months at a 36-month peak. At a 21% weight that implies about +10% on price. Steel adds +6.5% (about +1%) and labour +2.7% (about +0.5%), for a theoretical total near +11.5%. Steel is still -6.3% below its 36-month peak and -26.7% below its 2022 high.

Vesmo itself stated that its copper is bought forward at fixed prices until March 2027 and called the market price 'not our reality'. Its current quotes hold the 2026 price for 90 days, citing material cover. The copper rise therefore does not reach its costs before about April 2027, which argues for holding the price flat through the 2027 calendar year or at least until March. Expect it to push for an index clause or an increase from Q2 2027.

Price history moved 2023→2024 -2.6%, then +1.4% and +1.2%, so 2026 is back exactly at the 2023 level on both parts. It has settled well below its asks (last renewals: asked +3.5% / +4.3%, settled +1.2%). Changes above 2% need its pricing committee, which meets every two weeks.

Competition. On part:350010 Vesmo is cheaper than Nordmark: Nordmark quoted 245.59 in its 2025 RFQ and is current at 239.21, against Vesmo's 225.61. Vesmo is the cheap 30% source, so shifting quota to it is a lever for us, not a threat. On part:350012 Nordmark quoted 709.85 (+18%) and has 0% quota, so Vesmo is effectively sole source with no credible price alternative.

Other cost context. Industrial power is -43% vs 2022, a modest offset to conversion cost. Quality has worsened (764 ppm vs a 457 peer median) and on-time delivery is 81.1%; neither is a price driver, but both give non-price trade material.

findings.text: Copper is hedged: Vesmo states in writing and orally that its copper is bought forward at fixed prices until March 2027 and that the market price is 'not our reality' before then. This is a self-admission that defuses any copper-driven increase (CU-NOTATION +47.7%, ~+10% on price) for the 2027 price year at least through Q1 2027.

Approval ladder: price changes above 2% need their pricing committee, which meets every two weeks (stated at two annual reviews). The KAM can settle at or below 2% alone; larger moves cost time. We should plan rounds around the committee rhythm and expect slow steps on anything above 2%.

Deprioritisation risk: their sales director said they are reviewing small accounts and will focus on customers with volume. We are about 1.2% of their EUR 192M turnover. Volume is their lever and need. Our rising forecast (350010 +7.6%, 350012 +15.6%) is the counter-signal to offer.

Financially sound, group-owned company with stable credit (index 173 unchanged, equity 37.4%, VDA 6.3 grade A). There is no sign of distress, so no margin-rescue argument applies. They can afford to walk away from a small account.

Performance is slipping: on-time delivery is 81.1% against a 95% target (86.0% a year ago). Quality is 764 ppm against 203 ppm a year ago, with one 8D still open on 350012. This weakens any claim for recognition or a premium.

We pay reliably: on average 2.9 days late, never more than 9 days, and no discount abuse. Cash does not appear to be a pain point, though they may still ask for faster payment than the current 45 days.

Their style is formal and process-driven, with short informational letters. They also made a unilateral operational change (returnable boxes from November 2025), which shows they run a cost and efficiency agenda. Evidence on individual decision-makers is thin: we only know of a KAM and a sales director.

findings.text: Framework agreement ctr:4600070520 covers both motors (4 kW part:350010, 15 kW part:350012), runs to 2026-12-31 and auto-extends 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice. The termination window closes 2026-10-02, so a credible exit is open only for days. After that, 2027 runs under the same frame.

Prices are fixed per calendar year. Any change needs written notice at least 90 days before year end, i.e. by about 2026-10-02. A 2027 increase not notified in time has no contractual basis, and we should check whether Vesmo has notified. There is no index clause in the contract, so a copper index clause would be a new concession from us.

Payment is 45 days net against our 60-day standard, which already favours Vesmo. Delivery is FCA with a 42-day lead time, so we bear the freight. The quality agreement sets a 95% on-time target and a flat EUR 150 per supplier-caused complaint.

Renewal history is consistent across both parts. Vesmo asked -0.7/+4.7/+3.5% (350010) and -0.9/+2.7/+4.3% (350012) and settled -2.6/+1.4/+1.2%. Settlements land about 2-3 pp below the ask and never above about 1.4%. The price is back exactly at its 2023 level (225.61 / 601.27). The KAM said changes above 2% need pricing-committee approval, which makes about 2% the likely ceiling.

Dependency is asymmetric by part. On 350010 we are not dependent: Nordmark already holds 70%, although it is about 6% dearer per our current orders. On 350012 Vesmo is the sole active source (100%), Nordmark is only qualified, and Nordmark's last RFQ was 18% dearer, so we are effectively dependent there. Tooling is n/a in the master data, but the library claims supplier-owned tooling; the evidence conflicts.

We are a small customer: about EUR 2.2 M, or 1.2% of a EUR 192 M turnover. Vesmo is financially sound and has said it will focus on customers with volume. Our forecast volume growth (+8% / +16%) is our main currency to offer.

Performance is below contract. On-time delivery is 81.1% against the 95% target. Quality worsened to 764 ppm from 203 ppm, with 3 complaints on 350012 and one 8D still open. Vesmo's copper is bought forward until March 2027, which undercuts a copper-driven increase for 2027.

findings.text: Delivery is deteriorating steadily. Rolling OTD against the requested date fell from 91.1% (2024Q3) to 81.1% (2026Q3), and against its own confirmed date from 91.1% to 83.0%. The contractual target is 95% and the peer median is 84.6%, so Vesmo is now below its peers. In the last 12 months 18.9% of receipts were late, on average 15.5 days, at most 28 days. The scorecard class is still A/green, which flatters it.

By part, the 4 kW motor part:350010 is the worse deliverer: 77.8% on time against requested, 22.2% late. The 15 kW motor part:350012 is late less often (15.4%) but by longer when it is late (19.2 days on average). The delivery data carries a known data issue: requested and first confirmed dates differ by 10-30 points (KNOWN_ISSUES 1). The confirmed-date figure (83.0%) is therefore the safer one to cite.

Quality has reversed. Rolling ppm went from 0 (2025Q4) to 764 (2026Q3) on 4 complaints, against a peer median of 457 ppm; a year earlier it was 203 ppm. The rise is concentrated on part:350012: three different defects in six months (coating, leakage at test, missing marking), 1085 ppm over the last 12 months. qn:20004999 has no 8D closure yet. Recharges are only EUR 150 per complaint under the flat fee, so the true cost to us is likely understated.

On part:350010, Vesmo's quality is worse than the other source. Vesmo runs 405 ppm over the last 12 months against 180 ppm for sup:70510. Vesmo's defects there are recurring dimension issues (qn:20004352, qn:20004793).

Our volume outlook is growing and has been shared with the supplier. The 4 kW forecast is 8490 pcs over the next 12 months against 7890 ordered (all sources; Vesmo's share is about 30%, roughly 2400/yr). The 15 kW forecast is 3030 pcs against 2622 ordered, all of it Vesmo's. This matters because Vesmo said in April 2026 it will focus on customers with volume. Our spend of about EUR 2.2M is only about 1.2% of its turnover, so we are small to it. The volume growth is real leverage, but modest.

Prices are back exactly at their 2023 level after a dip in 2024: 225.61 for the 4 kW and 601.27 for the 15 kW. Our should-cost puts both only about 2% above cost, and that estimate carries roughly 5% error. On part:350010 Vesmo is 6% cheaper than sup:70510, so its price is competitive. This means price pressure must rest on performance, not on margin.

arguments.text: Our prices are already at or near cost: on the 4 kW motor we are about EUR 14 below Nordmark (225.61 vs 239.21), and on the 15 kW motor the qualified alternative quoted about 13% above us. Your own benchmarks confirm we are the cost-efficient source, so asking for a price-down means asking a key supplier to work at a loss.

We have shown restraint. Our 2027 quotes hold 2026 prices flat even though copper is +48% year on year and at a 36-month peak, steel is up 6-7% and labour 2.7%. Our forward cover lets us absorb this until March 2027 and no longer, which we have told you openly and in writing.
Since 2024 our settlements have stayed well below inflation and our asks (+1.4% and +1.2% after -2.6%). Cumulatively our prices are back at their 2023 level. We have carried the cost gap.
From April 2027 a copper index clause is the fair mechanism. Copper is about 21% of motor cost, and without a clause we would have to build a risk premium into a fixed price.
We are a stable partner: equity ratio 37%, unchanged credit index, VDA 6.3 grade A, ISO 9001/14001. We switched to returnable packaging at our own cost.

weak_points: Delivery has slipped every quarter: OTD fell from 91% to 81%, against a 95% contract target, with up to 28 days late.
ppm on the 15 kW motor is about 1085 in the last 12 months, with 3 complaints in 2026. QN 20004999 has no 8D closure (d8) yet.
Copper is hedged until March 2027, so cost drivers cannot justify any increase before Q2 2027. We said so ourselves.
Should-cost puts the 15 kW price only about 1.7% above cost, so they know our margin. Conversely, on the 4 kW motor they see about 2% headroom too.
Our KAM can only move about 2% without the committee, so they may exploit the delay.
The small-account review signals they could be deprioritised, which gives them a reason to suspect our service.
Electricity is down 43% versus 2022, which undercuts any energy cost claim.
The 90-day notice deadline (early October) for 2027 price changes is ours to miss. If it passes, prices stay fixed per year.
wants: A move of 4 kW quota from Nordmark toward us (e.g. 50%+). For this I would hold prices flat and possibly give 1-2%.
A 2-3 year extension with binding annual volumes on both motors.
A copper index clause from April 2027 with a defined base and a symmetric band. In return I would hold the base price fixed through 2027.
Binding forecast or call-off schedules to fix our delivery problem.
No price-down request on the 15 kW motor while we stay sole source.
red_lines: No price reduction below current levels on the 15 kW motor, which is near cost.
No fixed price beyond March 2027 without a copper clause or a step increase.
No chargeback above the EUR 150 flat fee unless we get price or volume relief.
No ppm or OTD penalty commitments without a realistic ramp-up period.
red_team.opening: Thank Hollerau for the growing forecast and acknowledge that our recent delivery performance is not acceptable, and present a recovery plan. Confirm flat prices of 225.61 and 601.27 through March 2027, stressing that we hold them despite copper at +48%. Propose a 2-year extension from April 2027 with a copper index clause, or alternatively a step of about 4%, linked to a higher 4 kW quota and binding volumes. Signal openness to trade.

rebuttals.answer: We agree that your prices are competitive, and we value that. We are not asking you to work at a loss. Our own estimate of your plant's cost puts both motors only slightly above cost, which is exactly why we are seeking a stable price rather than a cut. Competitive pricing is a reason to keep prices where they are, and our growing, shared volumes are what we can add to make that worthwhile for you.

We appreciate your openness about the copper cover; it is the kind of transparency that makes a long relationship work. By your own letter and our call, market copper does not reach your costs before the cover ends. A flat price for that period therefore reflects your actual cost position, not a sacrifice. Labour and steel are real, but their weight in a motor is modest and adds little to the price.

It is true that recent settlements were moderate, and we recognise that. The same record also shows that today's prices are the highest we have paid in this period, after an earlier reduction was fully recovered. Prices returning to their earlier level is a settled outcome we both signed, not an open gap still waiting to be closed.

We are open to discussing a copper mechanism for the period after your cover ends, rather than a risk premium built into a fixed price. It should start only once your hedge expires and use a base reflecting the current copper level, so that it works in both directions. It should apply to the copper share alone. Under our contract, prices remain fixed for the calendar year in any case.

We value your stability and certifications, and the returnable packaging was welcome. A strong partner is what we want to grow with. We would like to put a joint improvement plan, with a quality commitment, alongside the price discussion.

press: Since your copper is covered at fixed prices until your cover ends, we assume the quoted prices hold flat for the full period your letter describes, and we would welcome your confirmation.
On-time delivery has declined for several quarters and sits below our contract target; could we agree on concrete steps and a delivery commitment together?
Our shared forecasts show growing need on both motors, and we would like to discuss how a longer binding commitment could secure priority capacity for us.
As energy costs for industry have eased considerably, we do not expect energy to play a part in next year's pricing.
